Marsh tit (Poecile palustris) reproductive output is modest yet consistent across its range. The species lays a single set of eggs each year, with females producing precisely 8.5 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 8.5 eggs per clutch] and only ever raising one clutch annually [F_R_i = one clutch annually]. This annual reproductive investment, while moderate, is sustained during the active breeding season when internal body temperatures of foraging adults typically reach 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], reflecting the high metabolic demands of provisioning. The eggs themselves are incubated within a nest cup, and the duration of embryonic development is tightly coupled to thermal conditions. When the incubating parent maintains a stable nest temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C], the incubation period lasts 14 days [ab = 14 days] before hatching occurs. This relatively short incubation interval, comparable to that of other small parids, ensures that the altricial nestlings emerge before peak food availability wanes.

Upon hatching, the neonate emerges at a remarkably small body size. The initial wet body mass of a newly hatched Marsh tit chick is approximately 0.99 grams [Ww0 = approximately 0.99 grams]. This starting mass, calculated as 0.8 multiplied by 1.24 grams, yields approximately 0.99 grams [Ww0 = approximately 0.99 grams], though field measurements typically round to the nearest hundredth of a gram. This minimal starting mass imposes an immediate and intense demand for frequent parental provisioning with protein-rich insect prey. The delicate, nearly naked hatchling must rapidly gain mass over the subsequent days while being brooded to maintain thermoregulation. Growth is exponential during this early nestling phase, and the chick more than doubles its weight within its first week of life as the developing feather tracts emerge and the digestive system matures to handle the incoming food boluses delivered by both parents throughout daylight hours.

The nestling period culminates in fledging, a critical developmental milestone marking the chick's first flight from the nest. Under the typical active metabolic temperatures sustained by brooding adults, which hover near 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], the time since birth at fledging is 18 days [tx = 18 days]. This fledging interval is relatively brief for a passerine of its size, allowing young Marsh tits to leave the vulnerable nest cavity before terrestrial predators can locate the brood. After fledging, the young remain dependent on parental feeding for another two to three weeks while their flight muscles strengthen and their foraging skills improve. The 18-day nestling duration is a product of intense parental care, with both adults making hundreds of feeding visits daily to satisfy the energetic requirements of the growing chicks, which triple their body mass during this period.

Sexual maturation in the Marsh tit is a relatively rapid process once the juvenile transitions through its first prebasic molt. The time since birth at puberty, representing the onset of gonadal activation in young birds, is 54 days [tp = 54 days], occurring under the same elevated body temperature regime of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C] typical of active passerines. However, despite achieving this physiological readiness during their first summer, most young Marsh tits do not immediately breed. Instead, they delay their first reproductive attempt until the following spring, a pattern that underscores the importance of behavioral and social factors such as territory acquisition and pair formation. The 54-day interval to puberty is shorter than that observed in many other temperate-zone passerines, suggesting a selective advantage for early gonadal recrudescence that allows young birds to be physiologically prepared if an opportunity to breed arises late in the season.

Adult body size in the Marsh tit stabilizes after the completion of the first prebasic molt, with the ultimate wet weight of a mature individual averaging 11.9 grams [Wwi = 11.9 grams]. This mass is characteristic of small parids inhabiting deciduous woodlands, and it represents a roughly twelve-fold increase from the initial hatchling mass. The timing of the first brood is tightly linked to spring phenology, occurring precisely one year after the individual's own birth, or at a time since birth at first brood of 365 days [tR = 365 days], again under the body temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C] typical of an actively foraging adult. Maximum longevity in the wild has been estimated through recapture data, with the oldest documented individuals reaching a lifespan of approximately 13.2 years [am = approximately 13.2 years] at 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This considerable longevity is notable for a bird of this size and is thought to reflect the species' reliance on stable, resource-rich deciduous forests where cached food supplies buffer against winter mortality.
